title: How to do legal research with AI
description: Answer a legal question, brief a new instrument, or compare jurisdictions, with the authority and the checking handled the way legal work needs.
introduction: Lawyers don't distrust AI research because it isn't useful. They distrust it because a made-up citation looks exactly like a real one. Find that out in front of a judge, and no amount of time saved was worth it.

So the real question isn't whether a companion can find the law. It's whether it works the way you already do. Jurisdiction settled before anything else. Commentary first, then the primary law. Binding authority kept apart from persuasive. And every citation checked against the source, not against a summary of it.
Strawberry works in your browser, so it can use the databases you already pay for. It follows a citation into the source instead of stopping at the search result.

sections.title: Answer a question about the law

blocks.text: A rule from the wrong jurisdiction is worse than no answer. It still looks like an answer. So nothing gets searched until that's settled:

items: You name the jurisdiction, and it gets on with it. If the facts point somewhere else, it says so.
You don't name one, and it asks first.

You're not sure which applies, and it works that out from where the parties are, where the contract was formed, and where the harm happened. Then it checks that reasoning with you before going further.

blocks.text: From there it researches the way you were taught. Commentary first, to find the landscape and the authorities that actually control it. Then the statutes and cases that settle the question.

Everything comes back labelled: which jurisdiction, primary or secondary, binding on you or merely persuasive. A persuasive case from somewhere else can still be worth having on a novel question. It just arrives marked as one.
Your matter stays out of the search box, by the way. It searches the concept, not your client.

items.context: Research this legal question in my jurisdiction.

sections.title: Understand what a new law requires

blocks.text: Something lands, and the questions are immediately practical. Does this apply to us? What do we have to do? By when? Most of that work is scope rather than summary. The thresholds and exemptions are what decide whether you're in or out.
The same instrument comes back pitched at whoever has to read it:

rows: A specialist
Full detail, article-level references, no hand-holding
A client
Plain language, what they need to do, terms defined
A board
One page, the headline risk, and the number

blocks.text: Binding law, guidance, and proposals stay clearly apart throughout. People act on proposals as though they were already in force, and that's worth heading off.

items.context: Brief me on this new instrument and what it requires.

sections.title: Compare the rules across your markets

blocks.text: One question across five regimes is really five questions. The usual shortcut is to research the first one properly and then go looking for its features in the others, which quietly reshapes one regime to look like another.

So each jurisdiction gets its own researcher, working independently. They share no context, which is the point: nothing from the German answer can quietly colour the French one. Their findings get synthesised afterwards. It's faster than working through them in sequence, and it's the one part of legal research where running things in parallel genuinely improves the answer rather than just the speed.
Then the columns get normalised, because plenty of things look comparable and aren't:

items: Thresholds that are measured on different bases.
Penalties written as a fixed cap in one place and a percentage of turnover in another.
Dates that mean "in force" in one column and "applicable from" in the next.

blocks.text: Where a difference won't normalise, it stays visible instead of being tidied into a cell. What you usually want at the end is the strictest position on each row, because that's what a single global policy has to satisfy.

items.context: Compare this question across these jurisdictions.

sections.title: Know who you are dealing with

blocks.text: Plenty of legal work turns on the organisation rather than the law. A counterparty before a deal, a supplier before you sign, the other side before you advise. That's company research with the sources kept attached, and it's the same companion doing it.

items.context: Research this organization as a counterparty.

sections.title: The seven ways AI legal research goes wrong

blocks.text: AI legal research fails in a small number of predictable ways. They're worth naming, because the workflow is built around heading off each one rather than hoping for the best.

rows: Invented sources. The most dangerous one, because a fake citation looks exactly like a real one.
Every source needs a URL or a database reference. Anything that can't be located is flagged as unverified, never quietly included.
Invented pinpoints. The case is real, the paragraph number isn't.
Quotations get pulled from the actual text rather than written from memory. Page numbers that can't be confirmed are marked approximate.
Jurisdictional drift. A rule from one system presented as though it applies in another.
Every rule is tagged with the jurisdiction it came from, in every output.
Outdated law. A statute since amended, a case since overruled.
Statutes get checked against the current version and cases for whether they still stand. In fast-moving areas, anything more than a couple of years old is flagged for a manual look.
Persuasive authority dressed as binding.
Each authority is labelled binding or persuasive for your jurisdiction, not left for you to infer.
A blog post cited as though it were the law.
Secondary source claims get traced back to the statute, case, or regulation, and that primary source is what gets cited.
Confidentiality slipping into a search query.
Client names, deal terms, and privileged facts never go into a search. It searches the concept instead.

blocks.text: You still verify. That doesn't change. The difference is that the draft arrives with the predictable traps already handled, so your check is a check rather than a rescue.

sections.title: Build it around your practice area

blocks.text: Most of the value turns up on the tenth matter rather than the first. Once a way of working is settled, it can be saved: the jurisdictions you work in, the sources you trust, your citation system, the shape of output you actually want.

Teams that go further build a companion around the practice area itself. The fifteen or twenty workflows that cover most of your matters, plus the regulatory landscape, the enforcement history, and samples of past work product so it knows what good looks like in your firm. That's real investment up front, and it tends to pay for itself somewhere around the tenth or fifteenth matter.

items.context: Turn our accepted research method into something the team can reuse.

blocks.text: For an area you track continuously, a Routine can watch agreed official sources and report only what has genuinely moved. Worth setting up once you know the sources, the cadence, and what counts as material.
